result.summary: Guided by a herdsman, the Spartans under Emperamus break into the Messenian stronghold of Eira in a rainstorm. After three days of desperate fighting the seer Theoclus dies, and Aristomenes leads the survivors out through the Spartan lines.

scenes.title: Night assault on Eira
scenes.summary: The Spartans climb into Eira by ladder in the dark and rain. Aristomenes and Theoclus rally the Messenians while secretly knowing the oracle dooms them.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk losing their last stronghold and their country.

scenes.title: Three days of battle
scenes.summary: At daybreak the Messenians, women included, fight with despair while the storm seems to favour the Spartans. Hecas rotates Spartan reserves, and the Messenians wear out.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians face exhaustion, enslavement and the loss of their homeland.

scenes.title: Death of Theoclus, retreat
scenes.summary: Theoclus tells Aristomenes the fall is fated, then dies fighting. Aristomenes gathers the survivors and the Spartans let them pass.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes must save the surviving Messenians, including women and children, from slaughter.

characters.name: Gyges
characters.description: Lydian driven from Smyrna, son of Dascylus

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses Lacedæmonians and Spartans for the same people.

notable_quotes.reason: Conveys the despair of defending the last inch of Messenian fatherland.
Theoclus's defiant last words before dying.

analysis.text: Fate and oracles dominate: the leaders know the prophecy dooms Messene yet keep fighting and hide the truth to preserve morale.
Pausanias recounts the end of the Second Messenian War, a founding tale of Messenian identity under Spartan domination.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias compares the Messenians to the Ionians of Smyrna who expelled the Lydians, drawing on the early history of Asia Minor.

language_notes.text: The Pythian Priestess is the Delphic oracle; her prophecy about the he-goat (the wild fig tree, called "goat-fig") said Messene would fall when a he-goat drank from the Neda.
Smyrna's resistance to Gyges, king of Lydia, is cited as an example of a small city defying a stronger power.
"Give destiny the go-by" means evade or slip past fate.
"Rearmen" are the men in the rear ranks, who could not reach the fighting.
"Burthen" is an archaic form of burden.
The wild fig tree refers to an earlier omen: its growth toward the Neda's water fulfilled the oracle's sign of Messene's fall.

context_notes.text: Emperamus was the Spartan commander; the herdsman was a Messenian who had deserted and guided the Spartans to Eira.
Eira was the Messenians' last mountain stronghold in the long Second Messenian War against Sparta.
Seers judged omens by direction; lightning on the right was taken as a favourable sign. Hecas was the Spartan seer.

literary_notes.text: The dogs' unusual barking acts as an omen, hinting at the disaster about to overwhelm the Messenians.
"Their last possession... their last inch of fatherland" piles up phrases to heighten pathos and finality.
The leaders know the oracle dooms Messene while the others still hope, so readers see the hopelessness the crowd cannot.
The storm, thunder and lightning seem to side with the Spartans, mirroring the Messenians' doom.
"Glutted his soul with slaughter" pictures vengeance as a feast, showing Theoclus's defiant, fated death.
